Inherited from Middle Norwegian bygsla (“lease, tenancy; right of lease”), ultimately derived from Old Norse byggja (“to let out; lend money at interest”) with the suffixal element -sl-, further from Proto-Germanic *bugjaną (“to deal, do business; buy, purchase”), of uncertain deeper origin.

1000104.etyen:
Internationalism, ultimately from the name of the town now known as Togoville, situated on the northern shore of Lake Togo. The name originally referred only to the town and was subsequently extended to the surrounding territory and, ultimately, the modern country.
It is commonly analysed as Ewe to (“to pound”) + go (“shore”), literally “by the water”. During the German colonial period, the name was also used in Togoland, the name of the German protectorate.
Parallel international forms include Norwegian Nynorsk Togo, Danish Togo, Swedish Togo, German Togo and French Togo.

en.g: a male given name from German, equivalent to English John

1000360.etyen:
Derived from German Johan (“male given name”), a short form of Johannes (“male given name”), ultimately from Latin Iōhannēs (“male given name”), from Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs, “male given name”), from Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yōḥānān, “Yahweh is gracious”).
Compare Danish Johan, Swedish Johan, Dutch Johan, German Johann, Faroese Jóhan and Icelandic Jóhann (“male given names”).

1002664.etyen:
PIE word

Probably borrowed from Spanish adiós (“goodbye, farewell”), from a (“to”) + Dios (“God”), literally “to God”, continuing Medieval Latin Medieval Latin ad Deum (“to God”). Latin ad (“to, toward”) is ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“near, at; to”), while Deum is the accusative singular of deus (“god”), from Proto-Italic *deiwos (“god, deity”), from Proto-Indo-European *deywós (“(sky) god”), itself derived from the Proto-Indo-European root *dyew- (“to shine; sky, heaven”). Doublet of adjø (“goodbye, farewell”).
Compare the related forms Danish adjøs,

en.g: a surname from habitational, from Norwegian farm names and places named Nes or traditionally spelled Næs

1004712.etyen:
A surname variant of Næs, with doubled final ⟨ss⟩. Ultimately from Norwegian farm names and places named Nes or traditionally spelled Næs, from the common noun nes (“headland, point of land”), from Old Norse nes (“headland, promontory”), from Proto-Germanic *nasją (“headland, cape”), itself derived from Proto-Germanic *nasō (“nose”).
Compare Danish Næs, Swedish Näs and English Ness (“surname and place-name element”).

1004968.etyen:
From Håvard (“male given name”) + -sen (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””), originally a patronymic meaning “son of Håvard”. The patronymic later became established as a hereditary surname.
The given name Håvard is inherited from Old Norse Hávarðr. The first element of the Old Norse name is uncertain, and has been interpreted either as hár (“high”) or as an element meaning “battle”. The second element is vǫrðr (“guard, guardian”), from Proto-Germanic *warduz (“guard”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to heed, watch”).
